title: German Sentence Parts in Year 6: A Guide for Parents Who Do Not Speak German

youtube.title: German Sentence Parts (Satzglieder) in Year 6: Guide for Non-German-Speaking Parents (Bavaria)
youtube.description:
For parents who do not speak German and whose child attends Jahrgangsstufe 6 at a Gymnasium in Bavaria. What the LehrplanPLUS curriculum expects in topic D6 4.2 Sprachliche Strukturen untersuchen about sentence parts (Satzglieder), the two tests the school uses (Umstellprobe and Frageprobe) shown in pictures, the German grammar terms your child brings home with their English meaning (Subjekt, Prädikat, Akkusativobjekt, Dativobjekt, Adverbiale, Attribut), the five typical mistakes, and how to practise at home without speaking German.

German terms in this video: Satzglied, Umstellprobe, Frageprobe, Subjekt, Prädikat, Objekt, Akkusativobjekt, Dativobjekt, Adverbiale, Attribut, Aussagesatz, Nebensatz, Komma, Stegreifaufgabe, Schulaufgabe.

The German version for parents (Eltern-Lektion) and the lesson for children (Lektion) are on this channel as well. Curriculum: LehrplanPLUS Gymnasium Bayern, Deutsch 6, Lernbereich 4.2.
youtube.pinnedComment: Which German grammar term puzzles you most? Ask in the comments and we will explain it in the next video.

chapters.title: What this is about
chapters.goal: You know what the curriculum expects and why sentence parts matter for the years ahead.

scenes.onScreenTitle: German sentence parts: a guide for international parents
scenes.narration: Your child comes home with homework in German grammar: underline the «Prädikat», name the «Dativobjekt». You may not even be able to read the sentence. The good news is that the method behind it is simple and visual. Two tests, a handful of names. This video gives you the method and the words in a little over ten minutes: what the Bavarian curriculum expects in Year six, «Jahrgangsstufe sechs», pupils aged about eleven to twelve, how the two tests work, the typical mistakes, and how to help at home.

scenes.onScreenTitle: The curriculum: D6 4.2 Sprachliche Strukturen untersuchen
bullets: LehrplanPLUS: the Bavarian curriculum for Gymnasium
Sentence parts: predicate, objects, adverbials, attributes
Also: word classes, active and passive, compound sentences
scenes.narration: The Bavarian curriculum is called the «LehrplanPLUS». In German for Year six, the topic belongs to «Sprachliche Strukturen untersuchen», examining the structures of the language. Sentence parts, «Satzglieder», sit there beside word classes, active and passive, tenses, and compound sentences. Sentence parts are practised most, because everything else rests on them. A child who finds the parts of a sentence reliably will later recognise main and subordinate clauses and place commas correctly, which German marks strictly.

bullets: Split a sentence into its parts with the rearranging test
Name subject, predicate and objects with the question test
Tell adverbials apart: time, place, manner, reason
Recognise attributes as parts of a sentence part
scenes.narration: Four things your child should be able to do. First: split a sentence into its parts with the rearranging test, the «Umstellprobe». Second: name the subject, the predicate and the objects with the question test, the «Frageprobe». Third: tell adverbials apart by meaning: time, place, manner, reason. Fourth: recognise an attribute, «Attribut», as part of a sentence part rather than a part of its own. Which of these appear in tests is decided by the teacher. Why does it matter beyond German? Latin and English at this school ask the very same questions.

chapters.title: The two tests, in pictures
chapters.goal: You understand the rearranging test and the question test and can follow your child's homework.

scenes.narration: In Bavaria children learn sentence parts through two tests, not through definitions. The rearranging test shows where a sentence part begins and ends. The question test gives it a name. One observation holds everything together: in a German statement the predicate, the verb, always stands in second position. Let us walk through the three steps with a sentence like the ones in your child's exercise book. The captions on screen are in German, exactly as the child sees them in class.

params.satz: Am Morgen/A/Wann? | füttert/P/Was tut sie? | Lena/S/Wer? | die Katze/O/Wen oder was? | im Garten/A/Wo?

scenes.narration: The sentence: «Am Morgen füttert Lena die Katze im Garten». In the morning, Lena feeds the cat in the garden. The rearranging test, «Umstellprobe», moves the parts around without changing the meaning: «Lena füttert am Morgen die Katze im Garten». Whatever moves together is one sentence part, one «Satzglied». In the morning stays together, the cat stays together, in the garden stays together. The blocks in the picture are exactly these units. Five blocks, five sentence parts.

params.satz: Am Morgen/A/Wann? | füttert/P/Was tut sie? | Lena/S/Wer? | die Katze/O/Wen oder was? | im Garten/A/Wo?

scenes.narration: The question test, «Frageprobe», gives every block a name. Who feeds? «Wer?» Lena: the subject, «Subjekt». What does Lena do? «Was tut sie?» She feeds: the predicate, «Prädikat». Whom or what does she feed? «Wen oder was?» The cat: the accusative object. When? «Wann?» In the morning. Where? «Wo?» In the garden: two adverbials. The German questions appear above the blocks. Your child is expected to know them by heart, and the same questions return in Latin.

params.satz: Am Morgen/A/Wann? | füttert/P/Was tut sie? | Lena/S/Wer? | die Katze/O/Wen oder was? | im Garten/A/Wo?

scenes.onScreenTitle: Step 3: the predicate in second position
scenes.narration: Here is the observation that holds everything together, and it is the biggest difference from English. In a German statement, an «Aussagesatz», the predicate stands in second position, whatever comes first. «Am Morgen füttert Lena». «Lena füttert am Morgen». The verb stays in slot two. English keeps the subject before the verb; German keeps the verb in second place and lets almost anything go first. Once your child knows this, the predicate is found instantly, and every other part is measured from it.

params.satz: Am Morgen/A/Wann? | füttert/P/Was tut sie? | Lena/S/Wer? | die Katze/O/Wen oder was? | im Garten/A/Wo?

scenes.onScreenTitle: The names of the sentence parts
scenes.narration: Finally the names under the blocks: «Adverbiale», «Prädikat», «Subjekt», «Objekt», «Adverbiale». These are the terms your child writes in exercises. Bavarian schools use the Latin-based terms in Year six, which is good news for you: subject, predicate, object and attribute are nearly the same words in English. Only two need learning: «Adverbiale» for an adverbial, and «Satzglied» for a sentence part. Primary school may have used German words such as «Satzgegenstand»; those are not wrong, but the Latin ones are the ones that stay.

chapters.title: The parts and their German names
chapters.goal: You recognise the German names of the sentence parts and the question that goes with each.

scenes.narration: Subject and predicate are found quickly. The real work of Year six lies in three groups: the objects, which differ by grammatical case, the adverbials, which differ by meaning, and the attributes, which are not sentence parts of their own at all. Each group has its question, and with that question every exercise can be solved. Here they are, with one example sentence each, read by the German voice.

params.satz: Gestern/A/Wann? | schenkte/P/Was tat sie? | mir/O/Wem? | Oma/S/Wer? | ein Buch/O/Wen oder was?

scenes.narration: «Gestern schenkte mir Oma ein Buch». Yesterday Grandma gave me a book. Two objects hide in this sentence. Whom or what did she give? «Wen oder was?» A book: the accusative object, «Akkusativobjekt». To whom? «Wem?» To me: the dative object, «Dativobjekt». The question decides the case, and the case decides the name. This is where German differs most from English, which has no visible cases, so expect this to take your child a while. Two rarer objects exist, the genitive and the prepositional object.

params.satz: Wir/S/Wer? | fahren/P/Was tun wir? | morgen/A/Wann? | mit dem Zug/A/Womit? | nach München/A/Wohin?

scenes.narration: «Wir fahren morgen mit dem Zug nach München». We are going to Munich by train tomorrow. Three adverbials in one sentence. When? «Wann?» Tomorrow: an adverbial of time. By what means? «Womit?» By train: manner. Where to? «Wohin?» To Munich: place. The fourth kind asks for the reason, «Warum?», why. Your child also learns the Latin labels temporal, lokal, modal and kausal, and they appear in exercises. The English words are almost identical, which helps.

params.satz: Der kleine Hund/S/Wer? | bellt/P/Was tut er? | laut/A/Wie?

scenes.narration: «Der kleine Hund bellt laut». The little dog barks loudly. The word «kleine», little, describes the dog more closely and is an attribute, «Attribut». The key point: an attribute is not a sentence part of its own but a part of one. The rearranging test proves it: «Laut bellt der kleine Hund». The attribute moves with its noun; it cannot be moved on its own. The question is «Was für ein?», what kind of. Attributes can be adjectives, genitives, or whole relative clauses.

scenes.question: Your child says: "Ich muss das Prädikat unterstreichen." What are they looking for, and where will they find it?
scenes.hint: Think of the block that never leaves its slot.
scenes.narration: A quick check for you. Your child looks at a sentence and says: «Ich muss das Prädikat unterstreichen». What are they looking for, and where in a German statement will they find it? Take a moment. You have seen the answer in the pictures of this chapter.

bullets: Prädikat = the predicate, the verb part
In a statement it stands in second position
Can be two parts: hat … gefüttert
scenes.narration: The «Prädikat» is the predicate, the verb part of the sentence, and in a German statement it stands in second position. So your child looks at the second slot: «Am Morgen füttert Lena», «Lena füttert am Morgen», the verb is always there. One thing to watch: the predicate can have two parts. In «Lena hat am Morgen die Katze gefüttert», has fed, the predicate is «hat» and «gefüttert» together, and the second part sits at the very end. Both parts must be underlined.

chapters.title: Five typical mistakes
chapters.goal: You recognise the common mistakes and know which question corrects them.

scenes.narration: Five mistakes are common in many classes. All five are exposed by one of the two tests, so it pays to ask the right question rather than give the answer. You can do that in English; your child applies the test in German. Here are the five, two at a time, each with the question that helps.

bullets: Word class mixed with sentence part: noun ≠ subject
Attribute counted as a sentence part of its own
Ask: what moves together in the rearranging test?
scenes.narration: Mistake one: mixing up word classes and sentence parts. A noun is a word class; a subject is a sentence part. «Die Katze» is a noun, but in our sentence it is the accusative object, not the subject. Ask: who is doing something? Mistake two: counting an attribute as a part of its own, so «der kleine Hund» becomes two parts. Ask: can you put «kleine» alone at the start of the sentence? It cannot be done, so it belongs to the subject.

bullets: Predicate too short: hat … gefüttert has two parts
Dative and accusative object swapped
Ask: Wem? or Wen oder was?
scenes.narration: Mistake three: the predicate is taken too short. In «Lena hat am Morgen die Katze gefüttert» the predicate has two parts, «hat» and «gefüttert», forming a bracket around the sentence. Ask: what has Lena done? The answer names both parts. Mistake four: dative and accusative swapped, often because the articles sound alike. «Der Lehrer gibt den Kindern ein Rätsel». Ask the two questions: to whom does he give it? «Den Kindern». Whom or what does he give? «Ein Rätsel».

bullets: Die Katze füttert Lena: new meaning, not a rearrangement
Parts only swap places; the meaning stays
Ask: does the sentence still say the same thing?
scenes.narration: Mistake five is subtle. In the rearranging test the parts may only swap places; the meaning must stay the same. «Die Katze füttert Lena» is a grammatical sentence, but now the cat is feeding Lena, which was not meant. Children sometimes take such a sentence as proof that the cat could be the subject. Ask: does the sentence still say the same thing? If not, it was not a rearrangement but a new sentence. You can judge this from a translation, without any German.

chapters.title: Helping at home, and what comes next
chapters.goal: You have a ten-minute routine that works without German, and you know what follows.

scenes.narration: You can help without speaking German, because the tests are mechanical and your child does the German part. Ten minutes a few times a week are enough. Here is a routine that works in many families, then a look at how this is tested and which topics come next.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Step 1: one sentence from the exercise book
bullets: Child reads a sentence aloud and translates it for you
Rearranging test: how many ways can it be moved?
Circle the blocks, then ask the German questions
scenes.narration: Step one: your child picks a sentence from the exercise book or a school text, reads it aloud and translates it for you. That alone is useful practice. Then the rearranging test: they move the parts around two or three times and circle what travels together. Then the question test, in German: «Wer?», «Was tut?», «Wen oder was?», «Wem?», «Wann?», «Wo?». You follow along with the translation. Three minutes, and exactly what the school asks for.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Step 2: let them explain, in any language
bullets: Why is „mir“ a dative object?
Why is „kleine“ not a sentence part?
The child explains with the test; you listen
scenes.narration: Step two: ask for the reason, not the answer, and let your child explain in English or in your language. Why is «mir» a dative object? Because it answers «Wem?», to whom. Why is «kleine» not a sentence part? Because it cannot move on its own in the rearranging test. A child who can explain a test has understood it. If your child recites a rule but cannot justify it, that is the signal to go back to the picture with the blocks.

bullets: Mark and name the sentence parts in a short text
Tell objects apart by case, adverbials by meaning
Recognise attributes; show the rearranging test in writing
Mostly short tests; the teacher decides
scenes.narration: How is this tested? In German the big written tests, «Schulaufgaben», are mostly essays. Grammar is usually checked in shorter tests, «Stegreifaufgaben», and sometimes as one part of a larger test. Typical tasks: mark and name the sentence parts in a short text, tell the objects apart by case, classify adverbials by meaning, recognise attributes, and show the rearranging test in writing. What exactly your child's teacher asks is their decision; the exercise book is the best guide.

scenes.onScreenTitle: What comes next: clauses and commas
bullets: Satzreihe: two main clauses, comma between them
Satzgefüge: main clause plus subordinate clause, comma
A subordinate clause can be a sentence part
Latin and English ask the same questions
scenes.narration: What comes next? In the same topic, compound sentences follow: the «Satzreihe», two main clauses, and the «Satzgefüge», a main clause with a subordinate clause, «Nebensatz». With them comes the comma, «Komma», which German places by rule, not by feel. A subordinate clause such as «weil es regnet», because it is raining, is itself a sentence part, an adverbial of reason. A child who knows sentence parts recognises such clauses and places the comma correctly. And Latin and English ask the very same questions, so this work pays off twice.

In short: you do not need German to help with sentence parts. Two tests do the work. Whatever moves together in the «Umstellprobe» is a «Satzglied». Whatever answers a question in the «Frageprobe» has its name: «Subjekt», «Prädikat», «Objekt», «Adverbiale». Let your child apply the tests and explain them in any language, and ask the right question when something goes wrong.
